By centralizing home control through Siri, the company aims to challenge established competitors and deepen its presence within the connected household.

articles.title: ★ X Once Again Marks the Spot
articles.author: John Gruber
articles.content:
By John Gruber
Upon taking the CEO helm last month, John Ternus began tweeting on X. He tweeted “hello”, posted an iPhone event eve teaser and then a promo video for the new products, celebrated Apple’s plethora of wins at the Emmys and launch day on Fifth Avenue, and commemorated the anniversary of Steve Jobs’s death.
X is the only place these posts go. Same for Greg Joswiak’s account. Lighthearted stuff too, like Cook “introducing” Ternus to Pikachu back in August. You may not like it that X has re-found its footing under Elon Musk’s ownership, but it has. I’m citing Apple executives here but they’re far from alone. There are hundreds of interesting people and accounts I follow that post on X very regularly and do not post anywhere else at all. As a word nerd I love Merriam-Webster’s account — fun, clever, smart posts every day. That’s just one example among hundreds. Here’s another. Fascinating new apps are being shown and discussed on X and nowhere else.
[Update: I stand corrected — Merriam-Webster does have an account on Bluesky. It contains a subset of the items they post to X. They’ve posted 34 original new tweets on X so far in October; only 10 on Bluesky. Plus on X they’ve chimed in with 11 clever and/or informative retweets from other accounts, including one from those notorious fascists at Sesame Street; there are zero of those on Bluesky. So while I regret the error of implying that Merriam-Webster posts exclusively on X, the 45-10 count for October to date proves my point just as well.]
I see more interesting posts on X than I do on Threads, Bluesky, and Mastodon combined. I wish that weren’t so but it is. Most people don’t want to think about politics so they don’t. Those people, when they want to participate in a Twitter-like social network, go to X.
And I can’t blame anyone. The only network that compares to X, size-wise, is Threads — but Threads’s algorithm is weirder than X’s now, and the content I see there is relatively boring. My Threads timeline is full of engagement bait without being engaging. And if you want to judge a platform by its owner, “I’m grossed out and/or appalled by Elon Musk so I’m going to Mark Zuckerberg’s joint” isn’t a way to avoid being grossed out and/or appalled by the owner. Bluesky and Mastodon are too small for most people to care about — and, worse, they are the networks where politics are, in my experience, unavoidable. You can have a discussion about cool new use cases and tools for AI on X and people just discuss the tools and use cases. On Bluesky and Mastodon it’s difficult to have such discussions without arguments from people who (a) believe all use of AI is unethical, and (b) will shove their viewpoints into your replies.
The culture on X today is remarkably friendly and inclusive. It is a cheerful place. That cheerfulness is another differentiator. If you believe the world is falling apart and doomed only to get worse, that our obvious and real problems cannot be surmounted, X is not the platform for you. If you think the world is full of fun and amazing people and things, that humanity’s defining feature is our collective ability to solve any problem, that the only time better to be alive than today is tomorrow, it might be.
If you have stayed away, or even just mostly away, from X for years and then come back, people just say things like “Hey, glad you’re back!” On the other networks, especially Mastodon, they tell you you’re “feeding Nazis” — by going to the platform where Tim Cook posts Pikachu videos. These people have either lost their minds or refuse to check their prior assumptions. (Most of the ones who chime in about it publicly are the lost-their-minds types.)
But the bigger problem is that there’s little action on Bluesky or, especially, Mastodon. There’s a lot of activity on Threads, but little action. There is action on X. I’ve said for years that Mastodon is my favorite of the bunch and in a way it still is, but really that’s because when I go there I don’t have to be diligent to avoid wasting time. I avoid wasting time on Mastodon because there’s so little of interest to see. That’s a feature — for me — but it certainly isn’t what most people are looking for in a Twitter-like posting platform. They want action. The action is on X.
Without any fanfare — perhaps to avoid his ire — X has de-Musked its algorithm. I stopped visiting at all when the algorithm there was putting Musk’s own tweets into my timeline, every time I checked, despite the fact that I never followed him. But they don’t do that anymore. I don’t see much politics of any kind in my timeline, and what I do see is from accounts I chose to follow. I see tech (including a lot of interesting breaking news), sports (including a lot of interesting videos and stats), and stupid stuff that’s actually funny. My only problem with X now is that I do have to pay attention to avoid wasting time when I visit.
Plus, in addition to the tweets, there are now many interesting people using X to post entire essays and blog posts. I wish that weren’t so, for multiple reasons (e.g., no RSS). But it is so.
If you returned from exile on a desert island and took a look at X today for the first time in a year, you might reasonably guess that Elon Musk got bored and sold it while you were away. I do think he got bored micromanaging it, but the rank muskiness that permeated the platform after he took over is — for now, at least — gone.
articles.summary:
Apple executives and other prominent figures are increasingly returning to X, as the platform experiences a resurgence in user engagement and a shift in its algorithmic content delivery.

### Key Points
- Apple CEO John Ternus and executive Greg Joswiak have begun using X to share company updates, product launches, and personal milestones.
- Data shows high activity levels on X compared to competitors like Bluesky, Mastodon, and Threads, which struggle with lower engagement or niche content.
- The platform has reportedly adjusted its algorithm to reduce the prominence of owner Elon Musk’s posts and minimize political content in user timelines.
- Users are increasingly utilizing X as a primary hub for tech news, sports updates, and long-form content, despite the lack of RSS support.
- Critics of alternative platforms argue that networks like Mastodon and Bluesky often suffer from unavoidable political discourse and smaller, less active user bases.

### Why it Matters
The return of high-profile corporate leaders to X signals a potential stabilization of the platform's influence despite ongoing controversies surrounding its ownership. This trend highlights the difficulty alternative social networks face in replicating the critical mass and real-time engagement that remain central to X's market position.

articles.title: The hidden tax on enterprise AI: Why data architecture is the ROI problem nobody budgeted for
articles.author: Gaurav Chawla
articles.content:
The hidden tax on enterprise AI: Why data architecture is the ROI problem nobody budgeted for
Many large companies have spent the past few years investing in artificial intelligence infrastructure, software and implementation. Boards approved the plans. Finance built the business cases. Procurement negotiated for computing capacity.
One question remained. How would they manage the data underneath those systems?
This isn’t the kind of failure that makes headlines yet. There is no major outage, breach or recall. Instead, it is a quiet, compounding drag that appears as unplanned headcount and slipping timelines. Talk to enough infrastructure leaders about what happened and you’ll hear the phrase “data gravity” more than once.
The scale of the problem is visible in the numbers. A 2025 report from MIT’s NANDA initiative found that 95% of enterprise generative AI pilots produced little or no measurable impact on the profit-and-loss statement. The report points to gaps in how companies integrate AI into their operations, not simply to model quality. Those numbers should change how companies build AI business cases: A successful pilot does not prove an organization can run the same system across its full data estate.
The assumption baked into the budget
Most enterprise AI architectures still assume that data will move to wherever the new platform lives. Pull the data into one place and the intelligence layer on top will just work. It’s a reasonable assumption, but it is almost never true at enterprise scale.
Enterprise data has gravity. Regulations dictate where some records may live. Sovereignty rules keep other datasets inside a jurisdiction, even when compute is cheaper somewhere else. Business units that spent a decade building governance around a dataset have little incentive to hand it to a new central store and sometimes have no legal path to do so. Applications built around their data can also break in expensive ways when someone tries to separate the two.
This is typically hidden in a proof of concept. It runs on a small, pre-cleaned slice of data. The costs appear later, when the program has to deal with the messy majority left out of the demo.
“Data gravity” is the idea that large accumulations of data pull applications towards them and not the other way around. The bigger the dataset, the more expensive it is to move. Transfer fees are only the beginning; latency, bandwidth, security controls and operational effort add to the bill before a model produces a useful answer.
Where the bill comes due
The cost does not usually show up as one line item. It shows up as dozens of small demands on teams that already have too much to manage. They have to build and maintain pipelines to move data out of systems that were never designed for that kind of traffic, reconcile each copy with the original when the source system changes, and apply the same governance controls wherever the data is stored. They also have to keep track of the extra datasets created for development, testing, analytics and training.
None of these tasks looks disastrous by itself. Together, they become a tax on the program—one that gets more expensive as the organization tries to scale it.
Why the invoice arrives late
The most dangerous part of this tax is its timing. It often appears 12 to 24 months after the platform is procured and the team is staffed, when initial success metrics have already been reported upward.
By then, contracts are signed, teams are hired and the direction is publicly committed. Unwinding a centralization-first architecture is far more expensive than designing around data gravity from the start. Compute is easy to identify and assign to a budget; pipeline maintenance, reconciliation, governance, security reviews and the staff needed to keep the system running are spread across different organizations.
The missing layer is context, not just storage
Many postmortems on stalled AI programs stop at “our data wasn’t ready.” That diagnosis is accurate but incomplete. The deeper issue is that organizations are trying to solve a context problem with a storage strategy.
A model does not need raw data dumped in front of it. It needs context: the ability to find the right record, cross-reference it against policy, respect access rules and work from information that is current rather than a snapshot from the week the project began. That does not come from a bigger warehouse. It comes from an enterprise-wide context layer: a consistent, governed way to discover, connect and retrieve information across systems and locations without requiring every source to hand its data to a central store.
The underlying records, metadata and vectors AI systems use to reason about meaning are not the same thing. Records remain constrained by regulation, sovereignty, ownership and the applications built around them. Metadata and vectors can help AI find and reason about those records without inheriting every constraint that keeps the source data where it lives.
The question is not how to get all data into one place. It is how to make the right context available wherever the data already lives, under whatever rules govern it. Enterprises that treat context, not consolidation, as what they are building avoid rebuilding the same tax under a different architecture two years later.
The four key questions to ask
Before signing off on a major AI infrastructure investment, an organization should be able to answer four basic questions: Which datasets are regulated or contractually restricted from moving? Who owns governance for each dataset today, and what happens when a copy exists elsewhere? How will those copies stay synchronized as source systems evolve? And can intelligence go to where the data already lives, or does the architecture require everything to be centralized? These questions do not choose the vendor for you, but they will shape the shortlist.
The right architecture choice and vendor selection will lead you to AI outcomes and automate your business processes faster and at lower cost. These questions enable data architecture to be a first-class line item in the AI business case, not a detail to resolve after the compute deal closes.
The real ROI problem
The industry’s instinct is to measure AI ROI in tokens, throughput and GPU utilization. Those metrics are useful for gauging compute efficiency, but they tell only half the story. The other constraint on enterprise AI value sits upstream of compute: whether the data feeding the model can be trusted, governed and kept current without an ever-growing tax on the people around it. Token length and GPU efficiency tell you what it costs to run a model. They do not tell you whether the model has the context it needs to make a good decision. That depends on whether the underlying data is accurate, current, governed and connected to the right business process. It is the context curated from the data that determines the accuracy of agentic actions and whether you are on the path towards becoming an AI native organization or drifting away from it.
Compute is a line item enterprises know how to budget for. Data gravity is the line item many are still discovering, usually long after the check clears. The companies that get the most from AI will be the ones that design their data architecture to serve the context agents needed without moving or centralizing the entire distributed state.
Gaurav Chawla is Dell Technologies Inc.’s Fellow and VP, chief technology officer. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

### Key Points

articles.title: Automating the ‘future of work’
articles.author: Jyoti Banthia
articles.content:
Capria Ventures, which manages assets worth about ₹2,000 crore, is sharpening its focus on enterprise artificial intelligence (AI), manufacturing automation and the broader ‘future of work’ opportunity. Starting off in 2013, the fund backed technology-led businesses that addressed the needs of India’s rising middle-class in the areas of education, healthcare and employment and, eventually, moved to enterprise productivity and industrial capabilities.
Surya Mantha, managing partner at Capria Ventures, discusses the fund’s investment strategy and exit opportunities.
Edited excerpts:
How has Capria’s investment thesis evolved over the years?
Our first fund focused on education, employment, healthcare and essential services. With our second fund, we sharpened our focus on job-tech, investing in platforms that improve worker discovery, matching and access to employment.
Today, our job-tech portfolio mobilises over 1.4 million gig workers each month, generating nearly ₹200 crore monthly earnings.
It reinforced our understanding of technology’s potential to improve productivity and help workers move into higher-skilled roles. Our thesis has since expanded to the broader ‘future of work’ opportunity, particularly enterprise AI and manufacturing automation.
What do you look for before investing in a startup?
For us, startup quality comes down to the founder. We look for people who understand the problem deeply, address a market with real potential and have the resilience to navigate difficult periods.
Beyond the founder, technology must deliver a meaningful advantage that can endure through proprietary intellectual property, unique data or deep industry knowledge. Customers must be willing to pay for the solution.
Where do you see the biggest underfunded opportunities in India?
Enterprise AI offers opportunities in supply-chain coordination, sales productivity and factory automation, where domain expertise and measurable customer value can create a competitive advantage.
Manufacturing is another significant opportunity. The China+1 shift gives India an opening, but companies must move up the value chain through engineering, automation and intellectual property-led production.
In health-tech, technology can extend clinical expertise, improve diagnostic accuracy and make quality healthcare more accessible beyond major cities.
What is your approach to capital deployment and exits?
Our first cheque ranges from ₹5 crore to ₹15 crore, and we plan to back around 25 companies from our current fund.
We also reserve capital for follow-on investments, prioritising companies with strong execution and sound unit economics.
Strategic acquisitions and secondary sales remain important exit routes, while IPOs have emerged as a more meaningful option in recent years. Our exits include Awign, acquired by Japan-based Mynavi Corporation; Lab in App; Predible Health; UE Life Sciences; and SalesKen.
Published on October 12, 2026

- The firm’s existing job-tech portfolio currently supports 1.4 million gig workers, generating nearly ₹200 crore in monthly earnings.
- Investment criteria focus on founder expertise, proprietary intellectual property, and solutions that provide measurable value to paying customers.
- The fund identifies significant growth potential in supply-chain coordination, factory automation, and health-tech solutions that expand clinical access.

### Why it Matters
This strategic pivot reflects a broader trend of venture capital firms moving toward industrial automation and AI-driven productivity tools to capture India's evolving manufacturing sector. By focusing on these high-growth areas, Capria Ventures aims to capitalize on the China+1 supply chain shift and the increasing demand for scalable enterprise technology.

articles.title: Honda Wants to Put a Robotic Lab Assistant on Future Commercial Space Stations
articles.author: Andy Tomaswick, Andy Tomaswick (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/andy-tomaswick)
articles.content:
As I’m writing this I’m able to stare out into my driveway at my trusty Honda Odyssey. Most of the public’s association with Honda is through their “mobility” products - i.e. their cars. But the company has an impressive track record of other technical achievements, not the least of which has been in robotics. Now, it’s teaming up with space infrastructure firm Redwire to develop an automated laboratory support system for use on future commercial space stations.
Ask anyone who’s ever worked on the International Space Station (ISS) and they will tell you the most limited resource is astronaut time. While they are aboard, the humans on the ISS have essentially every minute of every day planned out for them. And some of those minutes are taken up with very mundane things like scanning barcodes for inventory management or swapping out biological sample trays. Astronauts are some of the most highly educated people in the world, and their time is extraordinarily valuable - but they also have to handle basic laboratory maintenance tasks onboard space stations because there is literally no one else to do it.
In fact, time is a resource that even the ISS itself is running short on. NASA plans to deorbit the station, which is about the size of a football field, around 2030, crashing it into the remotest part of the Pacific Ocean. In its place, a crop of private companies, such as Axiom Space, Vast, and Orbital Reef are hoping to launch their own versions of space stations, in which NASA will be simply one customer among many.
While these modern outposts would be a technical step up from the ISS, they are also going to be much smaller, at least originally. Many will only have a crew of two or four astronauts, and many go long stretches without being crewed at all. In other words, to keep the microgravity scientific experiments running, operators will have to turn to automation.
That’s where the Honda / Redwire robot comes in. Redwire itself is providing a reaching/motion platform known as Space Technology Autonomous Agile Robotic Kit (STAARK), which is assumedly named after Iron Man, but with enough of a difference to keep Disney satisfied. Redwire itself already has plenty of experience in orbital research, and manages eight operational science facilities onboard the ISS currently. STAARK is designed to autonomously interact with and grab dynamic objects, and offers the “reach” part of the robotic assemblage.
Honda, on the other hand, is very good at detailed robotic manipulation. Readers of a certain generation might remember their ASIMO robot that used to wave happily at people at tech conferences. But since then they have concentrated on robotic grips. The current version of their robotic hand features independently articulated fingers, each equipped with tactile and force sensors. Those give the robot a sense of “touch” that makes sure it doesn’t either crush a sample vial or have it float out of reach.
It will still be awhile before we see this collaboration in action in space, though. In theory, some of the early commercial space stations, such as Haven-1 from Vast and Axiom Station from Axiom Space, could launch as early as next year. However, there haven’t been any announced agreements for any of them to adopt the Redwire / Honda robotic setup. To introduce the concept, the company released a press release, and will be attending the International Astronautical Congress (IAC), currently happening in Antalya, Turkey through October 9th.
Automation will undoubtedly play a major role in future space stations, and Honda / Redwire’s offering sounds appealing with its impressive technical capabilities. But it remains to be seen if that is what the burgeoning space automation industry will rally around, or whether another option would potentially better fit the bill. But as space becomes more commercial, competition to supply the “shovels” of the next round of microgravity scientific research will undoubtedly heat up.

articles.summary:
Honda is partnering with space infrastructure firm Redwire to develop an automated robotic system designed to manage laboratory tasks on future commercial space stations in low Earth orbit.

### Key Points
- The collaboration combines Redwire’s STAARK motion platform with Honda’s advanced robotic hand technology featuring tactile and force sensors.
- The system aims to automate mundane laboratory maintenance, such as inventory management and sample handling, to save valuable astronaut time.
- Future commercial space stations, including those planned by Axiom Space and Vast, will require automation due to smaller crew sizes and uncrewed periods.
- The technology is being showcased at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, Turkey, which runs through October 9.
- NASA plans to deorbit the International Space Station by 2030, shifting the focus toward private, automated orbital research facilities.

### Why it Matters
Automating routine laboratory tasks is essential for the economic viability of smaller, next-generation commercial space stations that cannot support large, full-time human crews. This partnership highlights the growing competition to provide critical infrastructure for the emerging commercial space economy as private entities replace government-run research outposts.

articles.title: Lenovo's tiny AI PC ditches the box, and it's the smartest form factor I've seen in years
articles.author: Joe Rice-Jones
articles.content:
Look, everyone knows that I love mini PCs. There's just something about the form factor that excites me, whether that's a Mac mini, or something more powerful designed for local LLM work. But I'll also be one of the first to say there aren't many innovative designs out there, since most mini PCs are just some sort of box.
Then the Lenovo Yoga Mini landed on my desk, looking like it literally came from outer space. This puck-shaped PC has a lot going for it, with a powerful Intel Core CPU, quiet cooling, and a snazzy light ring. It's designed to be seen, not stowed behind your monitor, and I like that. It's not the easiest thing to upgrade, and the RAM is soldered on, but it slaps harder than a puck in the NHL.
About this review: Lenovo provided the Yoga Mini used for this review and had no input into its content.
Lenovo Yoga Mini PC (Intel)

The Lenovo Yoga Mini PC is a puck-shaped PC that begs to be left on display. It has style, grace, and a powerful CPU to get work done.
- Excellent port selection for the form factor
- Built in fingerprint scanner, speaker, and microphones
- Impressive performance
- Expensive

Price, specs, and availability
The Lenovo Yoga Mini PC is available from Lenovo and major electronics retailers like Best Buy, starting at $999 for the Ultra Core 5 325 base model. That's not the one we were sent for review; however, ours is the more powerful Intel Core Ultra X7 358H, with 32GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. That's currently $1,712 on Lenovo, with a bundled wireless mouse and keyboard. The base model is currently $700 at Best Buy, making it a convincing alternative to the Mac mini (though you'd get more performance on the Apple side).

What I liked about the Lenovo Yoga Mini
This is one stylish circle
The Lenovo Yoga Mini will impress you from the second you take it out of the box, because I can't remember the last time I opened up a circular piece of tech that wasn't a smart speaker. Inside the puck-shaped housing, you get the power of a laptop, plus a better selection of ports, from a 2.5 GbE wired LAN port to Thunderbolt 4, HDMI 2.1, and a single USB-A port. You also get a fingerprint reader built into the power button, two microphones for clear calls, and a built-in accelerometer that lets you turn the top of the Yoga Mini into a customizable button, much like tapping the back of your iPhone to trigger features.
This device is made to live on your desk, within easy reach and view.
This device is made to live on your desk, within easy reach and view. After using a string of laptops with fingerprint scanners, it's one of my favorite things now, and I love that it's included on this mini PC.
And Panther Lake still impresses
We got the more capable Intel Core X7 358H version, and we plugged it into a 4K OLED for all the time we used it. It's slightly more capable than a few laptops I've tested with the same CPU inside; the mini PC's extra thickness gives it more space for cooling, and it shows.

articles.title: Crypto Gurus Concerned AI Is Poised to Crack Blockchain Math, Allowing Hackers to Steal Funds With Impunity
articles.author: Victor Tangermann
articles.content:
As tech companies continue to claim their AI models are capable of cracking some of the toughest problems that have stumped mathematicians for decades, the crypto community is starting to become uneasy.
As Business Insider reports, certain luminaries of the scene are concerned that AI could unlock blockchain wallets, whose public keys are currently protected by nearly ironclad mathematical computation.
“Yesterday’s OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us,” Ethereum researcher Justin Drake tweeted this week. “They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen.”
As a result, Drake called “upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for ‘bunker mode,'” recommending crypto holders to move their assets to “fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash,” or a cryptographic mathematical function that acts like a digital fingerprint.
While the precise threat of an AI model capable of cracking causing crypto armageddon remains unclear, the community has already been wary of a separate threat in the form of quantum computers, which experts warn could eventually break current encryption algorithms by drawing on a qubit-based architecture.
While Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin took a less alarmist tone when discussing these threats, he still argued that AI could eventually overtake quantum computers as the biggest threat to the crypto community.
“I don’t recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today,” he wrote in his own lengthy commentary on X. “But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.”
Even hashes may not hold and could “theoretically” be “broken too,” Buterin argued.
If AI were to ever achieve such capabilities, the stakes could be considerable. As CoinDesk reports, millions of Bitcoin sit in address with public keys that are visible to all on the blockchain.
Yet how much of a problem AI will actually pose remains debatable. Despite plenty of breathless media coverage about AI companies’ claims of a mathematical revolution thanks to AI, many experts have since cried foul, arguing that they have yet to actually provide sufficient and legible evidence.
“OpenAI is flooding us with claimed revolutionary breakthroughs,” University of Milan associate professor Valerio Capraro tweeted. “Yet nobody knows whether the proofs are correct or whether they prove what they claim to be proving.”
In a statement this week, the Association for Human Mathematics also undermined OpenAI’s recent claims.
“We reject OpenAI’s assertion that this release advances our subject, and we urge mathematicians and the public to view the value of this publication model with due skepticism,” they wrote.
In other words, the crypto community may be panicking over a distant or nonexistent threat.
At the same time, there have already been instances of AI-assisted attacks on crypto wallets, according to CoinDesk. However, instead of brute forcing their way in through mathematical computation, AI allowed the attackers to identify and exploit years-old firmware bugs that left certain wallets vulnerable.
If there’s one thing Buterin and Drake can agreed on, it’s that the community shouldn’t act recklessly. Buterin warned that crypto holders should “be careful” about migrating wallets from address to address for additional layers of security.
“I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined,” he admitted.
More on AI and math: Mathematicians React With Fury as OpenAI Releases Hundreds of New AI-Generated Proofs
articles.summary:
Ethereum researchers and industry leaders are debating whether rapid advancements in artificial intelligence could eventually threaten the cryptographic security protecting blockchain wallets and digital assets.

### Key Points
- Ethereum researcher Justin Drake has urged the blockchain industry to prepare for potential AI-driven threats by moving assets to addresses hidden behind cryptographic hashes.
- Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin acknowledged that AI-accelerated mathematics could pose a long-term risk to current encryption, though he cautioned against immediate, panicked wallet migrations.
- The Association for Human Mathematics and other experts have expressed skepticism regarding OpenAI’s recent claims of revolutionary breakthroughs in mathematical problem-solving.
- While AI has already been used to exploit firmware bugs in crypto wallets, there is currently no evidence that AI can bypass standard public key encryption.
- Buterin warned that the process of migrating funds between wallets carries its own significant risks, noting that he has lost more capital through botched transfers than through security hacks.

### Why it Matters
The potential for AI to compromise cryptographic security could fundamentally alter the risk profile of decentralized finance and long-term digital asset storage. While the immediate threat remains speculative, the industry must balance the need for proactive security upgrades against the dangers of hasty, error-prone migration strategies.
